design_detail: Online pilot survey (cross-sectional, on SurveyMonkey), open from 1 February to 31 March 2019, of police, fire and emergency medical services (EMS) workers. It was spread by a flyer with a link and QR code, sent with a cover letter and an email to 15 associations of first responders in New York and nationally (3 acknowledged and said they would share it), by flyers at the authors' universities and informally by first responders linked to those institutions. 247 responses; the analysis was limited to the 187 from responders serving New York State (92 in law enforcement; 95 in fire, EMS or both). Fifteen statements on fentanyl risk, each answered on six levels from strongly disagree to strongly agree and reported only as agree or disagree by occupation (Table 2), plus questions on knowledge (gloves, naloxone, protective equipment, information sources) and on demographics. Descriptive; no test results are reported. Published as a Brief Report; read in its typeset online-first version.
can_establish: What these 187 self-selected New York State responders answered in February and March 2019: the share who agreed that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly, overall and in law enforcement against fire and EMS; their answers to 14 other statements on fentanyl risk and protection; their choice of gloves; and the information sources they named.
cannot_establish: How common these beliefs were among New York State or US first responders (no sampling frame, 3 of 15 associations sharing the survey, an unknown base and no response rate); how strongly they were held (the six answer levels are reported only as agree or disagree); where any belief came from (sources were not linked to answers); what responders do at scenes; or whether the beliefs are right (the survey measured beliefs, not exposure or harm).

sample.recruitment: Convenience sample: a flyer with the survey link and QR code, with a posted cover letter and an email, went to 15 associations of fire, police and emergency medical technicians in New York and nationally, asking chiefs to tell their members; 3 acknowledged and said they would share it; flyers were also posted at the authors' universities, and first responders linked to those institutions shared it informally (PDF p. 2, Methods, 2nd paragraph; Results, 2nd paragraph). Agencies did not have to say whether they had shared it (PDF p. 2, Methods, 3rd paragraph).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: First responders. After collection the analysis was limited to the 187 responses from responders serving New York State, because no other state had more than 9 responses (PDF p. 2, Results, 1st paragraph); the other 60 responses (editors' subtraction, 247 − 187) are not described.
sample.demographics: Table 1 (PDF p. 2), by discipline and size of population served: law enforcement 92 (41 serving under 25,000 people, 25 serving 26,000 to 75,000, 9 serving 76,000 to 125,000, 3 serving 126,000 to 250,000 and 14 serving over 250,000); EMS 55 (27 serving over 250,000); fire and EMS dual role 25; fire 15. A majority of every discipline had more than 15 years of experience (no figures), and 53.5% had encountered fentanyl or suspected fentanyl at work (editors' calculation: 100 of 187) (PDF p. 2, Results, 4th paragraph). Age, sex and rank are not reported.
sample.attrition: Not applicable (one online survey). Every statement in Table 2 has answers from all 95 fire, EMS or dual-role respondents and all 92 in law enforcement; whether answers were required is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: Self-selected respondents reached through the few associations that chose to share the survey, flyers and personal networks; the authors say the study base cannot be known (PDF p. 4, Limitations, 2nd paragraph), so there is no response rate. People more interested in fentanyl safety, or close to the authors' institutions, may be over-represented; EMS respondents came mostly from large agencies (27 of 55 serving over 250,000 people).

exposure.measurement: Not an exposure study: the groups compared are occupations (law enforcement against fire, EMS or both), as reported by the respondents; 53.5% reported having encountered fentanyl or suspected fentanyl at work (self-report, not verified).
exposure.polysubstance: Not applicable (a survey of beliefs and knowledge).

comparison.controls: None outside the sample; Table 2 sets law enforcement (n = 92) beside fire, EMS or dual-role responders (n = 95), without tests.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Training received on fentanyl, years of experience by group, age, sex and rank are not reported; the statement that answers did not vary across demographics comes without figures (PDF p. 4, Discussion, 1st paragraph).

outcomes.instruments: A questionnaire the authors wrote from a literature review, which experts in EMS, fire and law enforcement are said to have validated for accuracy (no validity or reliability data): 15 statements on fentanyl risk answered on six levels (strongly disagree, disagree, slightly disagree, slightly agree, agree, strongly agree; no middle or do-not-know option), with further questions on knowledge (which gloves are proper, the answers including nitrile, latex and unsure; whether naloxone can treat fentanyl exposure; access to proper protective equipment; information sources, ticking all that apply) and on demographics (PDF p. 2, Methods, 1st paragraph; PDF pp. 2–3, Results). The statement on contact reads "Briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly" (Table 2, PDF p. 3).
outcomes.validity_norms: No validation data. Answers are judged against expert beliefs that are not listed statement by statement; for the contact statement the Discussion treats agreement as contrary to research (PDF p. 4).
outcomes.operationalization: Agreement with each statement, reported only as agree or disagree; the paper does not say how the six levels were grouped or how many respondents chose each, so slight and strong agreement cannot be told apart.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Not applicable as reported: no test results are printed, although the authors say some limited statistical tests were performed (PDF p. 2, Methods, 4th paragraph) and that answers did not vary across demographics (PDF p. 4).

analysis.effect_sizes: Counts and percentages only, with no intervals. Contact statement: agree 63 of 95 fire, EMS or dual-role respondents (66.3%) and 86 of 92 in law enforcement (93.5%); 79.7% of all responses in the Discussion (editors' check: 149 of 187; editors' Wilson 95% interval 73.3% to 84.8%; the difference between the groups is 27.2 percentage points, editors' Newcombe interval about 16.0 to 37.7). Breathing airborne fentanyl is dangerous: agree 86 of 95 (90.5%) and 92 of 92 (100%) (editors: 178 of 187, 95.2%). Hand sanitizer is safe after handling fentanyl: agree 37 of 95 (38.9%) and 24 of 92 (26.1%), 32.6% in all (editors: 61 of 187). Gloves: nitrile 61.5%, unsure 29.4%, latex 9.1% (editors: 115, 55 and 17 of 187). Naloxone can treat fentanyl exposure: 92% aware. Protective equipment: 76.1% of law enforcement believed they lacked access to proper equipment (editors: 70 of 92), and 55.8% of fire, EMS or dual-role responders believed they had it (editors: 53 of 95). Information sources (all that apply): seminars or courses 78.1%, department training 76.5%, federal agencies 67.4%, professional or labor organizations 46.0%, social media or internet pages 23.0%, news media 13.9% (editors: 146, 143, 126, 86, 43 and 26 of 187).
analysis.preregistration_detail: No protocol or registration is mentioned; the John Jay College of Criminal Justice Institutional Review Board granted an exemption (HRPP file 2018-1578), and an informed-consent statement opened the survey (PDF pp. 2, 4).
analysis.selective_reporting: The 15 statements are reported only as agree or disagree; of the knowledge questions only gloves, naloxone, protective equipment and information sources are reported, and the others are not described; the limited statistical tests mentioned are not reported; the 60 responses from outside New York State are set aside without description; and the percentages for gloves, naloxone, equipment and sources carry no denominators (they fit 187, 92 and 95; editors' check).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Among 187 self-selected New York State responders in February and March 2019, 79.7% agreed, at levels not reported, that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly: 93.5% in law enforcement and 66.3% in fire, EMS or both. Most also agreed that breathing airborne fentanyl is dangerous (all 92 in law enforcement); 32.6% agreed that hand sanitizer is safe after handling fentanyl; 61.5% chose nitrile gloves as proper (29.4% unsure, 9.1% latex); and most named seminars or courses and department training as information sources, 13.9% the news media.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and Conclusions say respondents generally agreed with expert risk perceptions, with lower agreement on hand sanitizer, glove type and skin exposure (PDF pp. 1, 4): accurate in direction, but the headline does not convey that about 4 in 5 agreed with the contact statement, against the experts' view as the authors present it. The Results claim some generalizability because New York State is diverse (PDF p. 2), which a self-selected sample with an unknown base cannot give. The Discussion suggests that miscommunication and misinformation may have led to the 79.7%, and the Conclusions a possible effect of overreliance on media reports (PDF p. 4), although only 13.9% named news media and 23.0% social media or internet pages, against 78.1% seminars or courses and 76.5% department training (PDF p. 3), and no answer was linked to its source. The Discussion also cites the ACMT and AACT position statement for the view that harm from touching fentanyl is rather a chronic or long-term issue for people who touch it regularly or for long periods (PDF p. 4), which that statement does not say (see reporting issues).

timeline.event: ACMT and AACT position statement, cited (reference 9) with a NIOSH training video (reference 8, published March 2019) for guidance that rates the likelihood of an overdose from skin contact with fentanyl as very low (PDF pp. 1, 5), and again for harm from touching being chronic (PDF p. 4), which it does not say.
This survey, February and March 2019; published online in 2019 (PDF pp. 1–2).
Winograd et al.: before overdose-response trainings in Missouri in 2019, about 1 in 5 of 140 responders answered False to a statement that they could overdose from touching fentanyl.

Attaway et al. cite this survey (as Persaud and Jennings, 2019) for nearly 80% of New York first responders believing that even briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly (Attaway et al., p. 2). The 79.7% figure is right, but the survey reported agreement at levels it does not give, with law enforcement at 93.5% and fire and EMS at 66.3%, and its statement says briefly, not even briefly.
del Pozo et al.: before trainings in Indiana in 2020 and 2021, 103 of 129 officers (79.8%) agreed that responders who encounter fentanyl are at great risk of overdose by touching or inhaling it.

replication.where_it_stands: About 4 in 5 agreeing with a statement on danger from touching fentanyl recurs in the baselines of two training surveys by another team, whose authors partly overlap (Missouri and Indiana), each with a different statement, and none of the three is a random sample. This is the only survey on file whose statement concerns death rather than overdose, and the only one that reports information sources as numbers, though not linked to the belief. No probability sample of first responders is on file.

funding.funder: No funding source for the work or the article, apart from administrative support from the Christian Regenhard Center for Emergency Response Studies (PDF p. 4).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: Both authors are at John Jay College of Criminal Justice (CUNY), New York, and Persaud also at SUNY Downstate Medical Center (PDF p. 4). Jennings conceived the study, Persaud designed the instrument, and Paul Landsbergis gave feedback on its design (PDF p. 4). The authors share no author with the other surveys on file. Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount.

what_would_settle_it: A survey of a random sample drawn from complete rosters of New York State (or US) police, fire and EMS staff, with a known response rate and follow-up of non-respondents, using tested statements reported at every answer level, asking separately about touching, breathing in and contact with the eyes or mouth, and linking each answer to the training and information sources the person received and to what they do at scenes.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: No frame: the survey was spread through 3 of 15 associations that agreed to share it, flyers and personal networks, so the population it represents is unknown.
A self-selected convenience sample; the 60 responses from outside New York State were set aside after collection.
187 gives a reasonably precise share for the respondents themselves (contact statement about 73% to 85%, editors' calculation), but the size was not planned and some groups are small (fire, 15).

domains.domain: 4. Study subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Discipline and population served are tabulated, but not age, sex, rank or training, and experience only as a majority with more than 15 years.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Every statement has answers from all 187 New York respondents.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods for identifying the condition
domains.note: The belief is measured directly, as agreement with a statement, but the statements were only checked by experts for accuracy, with no testing of validity or reliability, and the six levels were collapsed into agree or disagree without saying how.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: The same online questionnaire for everyone, with one response per device.
Counts with denominators by group suit a description, but there are no intervals, the tests mentioned are not reported, and percentages elsewhere lack denominators.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response rate managed appropriately
domains.note: The study base cannot be known, so no response rate exists, and non-response was not examined.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Appraised with the JBI prevalence checklist. The editors summarise the risk of bias as high for any estimate of how common these beliefs were among New York State first responders: a self-selected sample with no frame and no response rate, measured with untested statements collapsed into agree or disagree. The survey may be cited for what its 187 respondents answered (for example, 149 of 187 agreeing that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly, more often in law enforcement than in fire and EMS) and for the information sources they named; not for the share of first responders in general who hold the belief, for where the belief came from, for what responders do, or for whether touching fentanyl is dangerous.

key_findings.finding: Methods: the authors wrote the questionnaire from a literature review, and experts in EMS, fire and law enforcement are said to have validated it for accuracy; it had fifteen 6-point statements on risk perception (strongly disagree, disagree, slightly disagree, slightly agree, agree, strongly agree) and further questions on knowledge and demographics, with consent on its opening page. It ran on SurveyMonkey from 1 February to 31 March 2019, confidentially; a flyer with the link and a QR code went to 15 associations of fire, police and emergency medical technicians in New York and nationally (15 letters and 15 emails, asking chiefs to tell their members), flyers were posted at the authors' universities, and first responders linked to those institutions shared it; one response per device; the aim was mainly descriptive, with some limited statistical tests.

247 responses were received; 187 came from first responders serving New York State and no other state had more than 9, so the analysis was limited to New York. Of the 15 associations, 3 acknowledged and said they would share the survey; it took about 5 minutes to complete. Because agencies did not have to say whether they shared it, the authors cannot ascertain the overall study base.
key_findings.locator: Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs (PDF p. 2); Limitations, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Respondents by discipline (Table 1): law enforcement 92, EMS 55, fire and EMS dual role 25, fire 15 (187); the law enforcement respondents were spread fairly evenly across sizes of population served, while 27 of the 55 EMS respondents served populations over 250,000. A majority of all disciplines had more than 15 years of experience, and 53.5% had encountered fentanyl or suspected fentanyl at work.
key_findings.note: 53.5% fits 100 of 187 (editors' calculation); no figures are given for experience.

key_findings.finding: Briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly: agree 63 of 95 fire, EMS or dual-role respondents (66.3%), disagree 32 (33.7%); agree 86 of 92 in law enforcement (93.5%), disagree 6 (6.5%). The Discussion gives 79.7% of responses agreeing.
key_findings.locator: Table 2, row on briefly touching fentanyl (PDF p. 3); Discussion, 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: 149 of 187 = 79.7%, Wilson 95% interval 73.3% to 84.8%; the six levels are reported only as agree or disagree.

key_findings.finding: Other statements (agree, fire, EMS or dual role of 95; law enforcement of 92): breathing airborne fentanyl is dangerous to my health 86 (90.5%), 92 (100%); you should not touch your face after handling fentanyl 90 (94.7%), 91 (98.9%); it is safe to disturb fentanyl without protective equipment if you use caution 12 (12.6%), 5 (5.4%); fentanyl in pill form is safe to handle 40 (42.1%), 13 (14.1%); the only type of fentanyl that is a health risk to me is the powder form 17 (17.9%), 2 (2.2%); fentanyl has the same strength as morphine 16 (16.8%), 18 (19.6%); I can see the signs and symptoms of a fentanyl overdose 77 (81.1%), 71 (77.2%); it is safe to use hand sanitizer after handling fentanyl 37 (38.9%), 24 (26.1%); gloves should be changed regularly 83 (87.4%), 80 (87%); it is safe to eat, drink or smoke when handling fentanyl 3 (3.2%), 2 (2.2%); I would not be concerned about needing emergency treatment for exposure 26 (27.4%), 6 (6.5%); I would not be worried about having difficulty breathing 26 (27.4%), 2 (2.2%); I am concerned about covering my nose and mouth 68 (71.6%), 90 (97.8%); I am not worried about protecting my eyes and face 20 (21.1%), 3 (3.3%).

Protective measures: 92% knew that naloxone could be used to treat exposure to fentanyl; asked which gloves are proper for handling suspected fentanyl, 61.5% chose nitrile, 29.4% were unsure and 9.1% chose latex; 76.1% of law enforcement respondents believed they did not have access to proper protective equipment, while 55.8% of fire, EMS or dual-role respondents believed they did; fire and EMS respondents were nearly split on whether fentanyl in pill form is safe to handle (42.1% agreeing), while 85.9% of law enforcement disagreed.
key_findings.locator: Results › Protective Measures, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 2) and 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 2, continued on p. 3); 3rd paragraph (PDF p. 3)

key_findings.finding: Information sources on fentanyl exposure and safety (all that apply): seminars or courses 78.1%, department training 76.5%, federal agencies 67.4%, professional or labor organizations 46.0%, social media or internet pages 23.0% and news media 13.9%; the authors conclude that a sizable majority relies on official sources, specialized courses and departmental training being the most common.
key_findings.locator: Results › Information Sources, 1st paragraph (left column, continued in the right column)
key_findings.note: Sources were asked about fentanyl exposure and safety in general and are not linked to any answer, including the contact statement.

key_findings.finding: Discussion: respondents understood the need to protect the eyes, face, mouth and nose, and answers did not vary across demographics (no figures). The authors name four main issues: 32.6% agreeing that hand sanitizer is safe after fentanyl exposure (which, they write, would spread fentanyl and may increase absorption); 38.5% unable to identify nitrile as the proper glove; 79.7% agreeing that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly, which they suggest miscommunication and misinformation may have caused, writing that research has shown brief contact is not deadly and harms no one who washes the skin thoroughly with soap and water, and that harm from touching fentanyl is rather a chronic or long-term issue for people who touch it regularly or for long periods (citing reference 9); and law enforcement believing they lack proper protective equipment, while fire and EMS respondents believe they have it.
key_findings.locator: Discussion, 1st paragraph (PDF p. 3, continued on p. 4) and 2nd paragraph (PDF p. 4)
key_findings.note: Reference 9 is the ACMT and AACT position statement, which does not contain the chronic-harm statement (see reporting issues).

key_findings.finding: Introduction: initial concerns over hazards to responders may have been heightened by early warnings from law enforcement sources (reference 7, a Drug Enforcement Administration nationwide alert on fentanyl published in March 2015); since then, guidance from authoritative sources rates the likelihood of an overdose from skin contact with fentanyl as very low (reference 8, a NIOSH training video published in March 2019, and reference 9, the 2017 ACMT and AACT statement); and sensational media reports of often non-specific symptoms after casual exposure have become commonplace (reference 10, a New York Times editorial of April 2019).
key_findings.locator: Introduction (unheaded), 4th paragraph (PDF p. 1, right column); references 7 to 10 (PDF p. 5)
key_findings.note: The paper does not mention the Drug Enforcement Administration's roll-call training video that other papers on file date to 2016 (Attaway et al., 2021) or to 6 June 2017 (Herman et al., 2020).

key_findings.finding: Stated limitations: self-reported data, which some respondents may have given differently from their behaviour in the field; an online survey, chosen for confidentiality, that limited follow-up; the overall study base cannot be ascertained; and future studies should use in-person systematic sampling, wider samples in other states and nationally, follow-up interviews or focus groups, and paired items to check reliability. Conclusions: respondents generally agreed with expert risk perceptions, but not on hand sanitizer, glove type and skin exposure; larger samples are needed to validate the findings; the knowledge gaps reflect a need for better training through authoritative sources, and a possible effect of overreliance on media reports of adverse effects from casual exposure.

Funding: none, apart from administrative support from the Christian Regenhard Center for Emergency Response Studies; no conflict-of-interest statement; exempted by the John Jay College of Criminal Justice Institutional Review Board (HRPP file 2018-1578).
key_findings.locator: Funding; Institution and Ethics approval and informed consent

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion cites the 2017 ACMT and AACT position statement (reference 9) for the view that harm from touching fentanyl is rather a chronic or long-term issue, more likely in people who touch it regularly or for long periods (PDF p. 4). The statement on file contains no such passage; its opening position and its section on long-term effects say that, in the absence of prolonged lack of oxygen, no persistent effects are expected after exposure (Moss et al., 2017, PDF pp. 1, 4).
reporting_issues.consequence: The chronic-harm statement has no support in the source cited for it, and the paper should not be cited for it.

reporting_issues.issue: The 15 statements were answered on six levels but are reported only as agree or disagree, without saying how the levels were grouped or how many respondents chose each.
reporting_issues.consequence: The 79.7% agreeing that briefly touching fentanyl could be deadly cannot be split into strong and slight agreement, so how firmly the belief was held is unknown.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract says 3 of the 15 associations acknowledged and distributed the survey (PDF p. 1); the Results say 3 acknowledged and said they would distribute it (PDF p. 2), and the Methods that agencies did not have to say whether they had (PDF p. 2).
reporting_issues.consequence: Whether the 3 associations actually shared the survey, and with how many people, is unknown; no response rate can be computed.

reporting_issues.issue: Of the knowledge questions, only gloves, naloxone, protective equipment and information sources are reported; the limited statistical tests mentioned in the Methods are not reported; the statement that answers did not vary across demographics comes without figures; and the percentages for gloves, naloxone, equipment and sources have no stated denominators.
reporting_issues.consequence: Selective reporting cannot be ruled out; the counts behind the percentages can be recovered (they fit 187, 92 and 95; editors' check).
